questions.stem: How many chromosomes are normally present in a human somatic cell?
questions.initialExplanation: Human somatic cells are diploid and contain 46 chromosomes arranged in 23 pairs.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. 46 — Correct. A typical somatic cell contains 22 pairs of autosomes and one pair of sex chromosomes.
- B. 44 — Incorrect. This is the number of autosomes, excluding the two sex chromosomes.
- C. 23 — Incorrect. This is the haploid number found in normal gametes.
- D. 47 — Incorrect. This is the chromosome number in many trisomies, such as free trisomy 21.
- E. 92 — Incorrect. This is a tetraploid chromosome complement.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Somatic cells: diploid, 46 chromosomes.
- Gametes: haploid, 23 chromosomes.
- Typical karyotype: 46,XX or 46,XY.

questions.stem: A normal human ovum or sperm contains how many chromosomes?
questions.initialExplanation: Germ cells are haploid, carrying one chromosome from each homologous pair.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. 23 — Correct. The ovum contains 22 autosomes and an X chromosome; sperm contains 22 autosomes and either X or Y.
- B. 47 — Incorrect. This is an aneuploid complement.

- C. 46 — Incorrect. This is the usual somatic chromosome number.
- D. 44 — Incorrect. This is the autosome count in a diploid somatic cell.
- E. 22 — Incorrect. A gamete normally carries 22 autosomes plus one sex chromosome.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Meiosis reduces chromosome number from diploid to haploid.
- Fertilization restores the diploid number.
- The ovum contributes an X chromosome; sperm contributes X or Y.

questions.stem: Which structure joins the two sister chromatids of a replicated chromosome?
questions.correctAnswerText: Centromere
questions.initialExplanation: Sister chromatids are attached at the centromere, which is important for chromosome segregation during cell division.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Centromere — Correct. It is the primary constriction where sister chromatids are joined and the kinetochore forms.
- B. Locus — Incorrect. A locus is the position of a gene on a chromosome.
- C. p arm — Incorrect. The p arm is the short arm of a chromosome.
- D. Telomere — Incorrect. Telomeres are protective structures at chromosome ends.
- E. q arm — Incorrect. The q arm is the long arm of a chromosome.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- P = short arm; q = long arm.
- Centromere position is used to describe chromosome morphology.
- Telomeres protect chromosome ends.

questions.stem: What is the principal information obtained from conventional karyotyping?

options.label: A
options.text: Chromosome number and large-scale chromosome structure

options.label: E
options.text: DNA base sequence of each gene

questions.correctAnswerText: Chromosome number and large-scale chromosome structure
questions.initialExplanation: Karyotyping examines chromosome number, size, and shape and can identify many aneuploidies and large structural rearrangements.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Chromosome number and large structure — Correct. It can detect numerical abnormalities and sufficiently large structural changes.
- B. Serum proteins — Incorrect. These are measured by biochemical laboratory tests.
- C. Protein expression — Incorrect. This requires molecular or proteomic methods.
- D. Mitochondrial enzyme activity — Incorrect. This is not the purpose of karyotyping.

- E. Complete DNA sequence — Incorrect. This requires sequencing, not conventional karyotyping.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Karyotype notation includes chromosome number and sex chromosomes, e.g. 46,XX or 46,XY.
- Karyotyping detects aneuploidy and many large rearrangements.
- Small sequence variants and submicroscopic copy-number changes may be missed.

questions.stem: What is the main principle of fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH)?

options.label: A
options.text: Fluorescently labelled probes bind to complementary DNA sequences in cells or chromosomes

options.label: B
options.text: It amplifies most DNA without using probes

options.label: E
options.text: It measures the electrical activity of chromosomes

questions.correctAnswerText: Fluorescently labelled probes bind to complementary DNA sequences in cells or chromosomes
questions.initialExplanation: FISH uses fluorescent DNA probes to detect the presence, absence, or location of specific chromosomal regions or sequences.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Fluorescent probes — Correct. A probe hybridizes to a complementary target sequence and is visualized by fluorescence microscopy.
- B. Amplifies all DNA — Incorrect. PCR amplifies DNA; FISH localizes a selected sequence.
- C. Liver enzymes — Incorrect. These are assessed by liver function tests.
- D. Serum antibodies — Incorrect. FISH is a molecular cytogenetic technique, not an antibody test.
- E. Electrical activity — Incorrect. Chromosomes are not assessed by electrophysiological testing.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- FISH is targeted: it answers a question about a selected DNA/chromosome region.
- It can detect selected microdeletions or rearrangements when the correct probe is used.
- A normal result does not exclude every genetic disorder.

questions.stem: Which laboratory method is used to amplify a selected DNA segment for molecular analysis?
questions.correctAnswerText: Polymerase chain reaction (PCR)
questions.initialExplanation: PCR makes many copies of a selected DNA region, allowing subsequent analysis for specific genetic variants or pathogens.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. PCR — Correct. It amplifies a target DNA sequence using primers and DNA polymerase.
- B. CBC — Incorrect. This measures blood-cell parameters.

- C. Karyotyping — Incorrect. This visualizes chromosomes rather than amplifying a DNA segment.
- D. FISH — Incorrect. FISH detects the location or presence of a targeted sequence using probes; it is not the general DNA amplification method.
- E. Echocardiography — Incorrect. This evaluates cardiac structure and function.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- PCR = amplification of a selected nucleic-acid sequence.
- Karyotype = chromosome number/large structure.
- FISH = localization/detection of a selected DNA sequence.

questions.stem: Which child is an appropriate candidate for cytogenetic or genetic evaluation?

options.label: A
options.text: A healthy child with a single uncomplicated viral cold

options.label: B
options.text: A child with multiple congenital anomalies and dysmorphic features

options.label: C
options.text: A child with a transient low-grade fever

options.label: D
options.text: A child with a minor isolated bruise after known trauma

options.label: E
options.text: A child with normal development and no relevant family history or clinical concern

questions.correctAnswerText: A child with multiple congenital anomalies and dysmorphic features
questions.initialExplanation: Cytogenetic evaluation may be indicated in children with congenital anomalies, developmental delay, dysmorphism, ambiguous genitalia, or other findings suggesting a chromosomal disorder.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Viral cold — Incorrect. An uncomplicated acute infection is not an indication for cytogenetic testing.
- B. Multiple anomalies/dysmorphism — Correct. This is a recognized indication for genetics assessment and possible chromosome testing.
- C. Fever alone — Incorrect. A transient fever does not suggest a chromosome disorder.
- D. Known accidental bruise — Incorrect. This is not a genetics indication by itself.
- E. No concern — Incorrect. Routine cytogenetic testing is not indicated without a clinical reason.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Consider genetics assessment in developmental delay, dysmorphism, multiple congenital anomalies, and ambiguous genitalia.
- Prenatal indications include selected abnormal ultrasound or screening findings and relevant parental chromosome rearrangements.
- Choose the test based on the suspected abnormality and genetics advice.

## Types of Genetic Disorders and Chromosome Abnormalities

topics.name: Types of Genetic Disorders and Chromosome Abnormalities

questions.stem: Which group lists the major categories of genetic disease described?
questions.correctAnswerText: Chromosomal, single-gene, multifactorial, and mitochondrial
questions.initialExplanation: Genetic disorders can result from chromosome abnormalities, pathogenic variants in individual genes, complex gene-environment interactions, or mitochondrial DNA abnormalities.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Mixed terms — Incorrect. Bacterial, viral, and fungal refer to pathogens, not genetic disease categories.

- B. Etiological groupings — Incorrect. These do not describe standard guidance's genetic classification.
- C. Four genetic categories — Correct. This is the classification presented.
- D. Clinical disease groups — Incorrect. These are not the major genetic categories.
- E. Mixed categories — Incorrect. Infectious and inflammatory are not inheritance categories.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Chromosomal disorders: numerical or structural.
- Single-gene disorders: Mendelian inheritance patterns.
- Multifactorial disorders: multiple genetic and environmental contributors.
- Mitochondrial disorders: often maternal inheritance.

questions.stem: What is aneuploidy?

options.label: A
options.text: Inheritance of mitochondrial DNA from the father

options.label: B
options.text: A change in a single nucleotide

options.label: D
options.text: Gain of one or more complete sets of chromosomes

options.label: E
options.text: Gain or loss of one or more individual chromosomes

questions.correctAnswerText: Gain or loss of one or more individual chromosomes
questions.initialExplanation: Aneuploidy is an abnormal number of individual chromosomes, such as trisomy or monosomy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Paternal mitochondrial inheritance — Incorrect. Mitochondrial DNA is generally maternally inherited.

- B. Single nucleotide change — Incorrect. This is a sequence-level variant.
- C. Reversed chromosome segment — Incorrect. This is an inversion.
- D. Complete chromosome sets — Incorrect. This describes polyploidy, such as triploidy.
- E. Gain or loss of individual chromosomes — Correct. Examples include trisomy 21 and monosomy X.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Trisomy = one extra chromosome.
- Monosomy = one chromosome missing from a pair.
- Aneuploidy differs from polyploidy, which involves extra whole chromosome sets.

questions.stem: Which pairing is correct?

options.label: B
options.text: Down syndrome — trisomy 21; Turner syndrome — monosomy X

options.label: C
options.text: Down syndrome — triploidy; Turner syndrome — tetraploidy

options.label: D
options.text: Down syndrome — deletion 5p; Turner syndrome — trisomy 21

options.label: E
options.text: Down syndrome — monosomy 21; Turner syndrome — trisomy X

questions.correctAnswerText: Down syndrome — trisomy 21; Turner syndrome — monosomy X
questions.initialExplanation: The classic karyotypes are trisomy 21 for Down syndrome and 45,X for Turner syndrome, although mosaic and structural variants also occur.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Sex chromosome trisomies — Incorrect. 47,XXY is Klinefelter syndrome; 47,XXX is trisomy X.

- B. Correct pairing — Correct. These are the classic chromosome abnormalities.
- C. Polyploidy — Incorrect. Neither is classically caused by triploidy or tetraploidy.
- D. Incorrect rearrangements — Incorrect. Deletion 5p causes cri-du-chat syndrome.
- E. Reversed abnormalities — Incorrect. Turner syndrome is not trisomy X, and Down syndrome is not monosomy 21.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Down syndrome: usually trisomy 21.
- Turner syndrome: usually 45,X or a mosaic/structural variant.
- Confirm with an appropriate chromosome study.

questions.stem: What is chromosomal mosaicism?

options.label: A
options.text: Presence of two or more genetically distinct cell lines derived from one zygote

options.label: B
options.text: A chromosome segment is duplicated in each cell

options.label: C
options.text: most cells have an identical normal karyotype

options.label: D
options.text: A gene is inherited from the mother

options.label: E
options.text: A person has two different blood groups due to transfusion

questions.correctAnswerText: Presence of two or more genetically distinct cell lines derived from one zygote
questions.initialExplanation: Mosaicism occurs when a person has two or more cell populations with different chromosome complements, often because of a postzygotic mitotic error.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Multiple cell lines — Correct. For example, some cells may be 46,XX and others 47,XX,+21.
- B. Duplication in every cell — Incorrect. This describes a constitutional duplication rather than mosaicism.
- C. One normal cell line — Incorrect. This is not mosaicism.
- D. Maternal inheritance — Incorrect. This may describe mitochondrial inheritance, not chromosomal mosaicism.
- E. Blood group after transfusion — Incorrect. This is not the genetic definition of mosaicism.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Mosaicism can modify phenotype and severity.
- The proportion of abnormal cells may differ between tissues.
- A blood karyotype may not always reflect every tissue's cell lines.

questions.stem: Which structural chromosome abnormality involves loss of a chromosome segment?
questions.correctAnswerText: Deletion
questions.initialExplanation: Deletion is the loss of a chromosome segment and may cause disease through loss of genetic material.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Deletion — Correct. A portion of a chromosome is missing.
- B. Triploidy — Incorrect. This is a numerical whole-set abnormality.

- C. Inversion — Incorrect. A segment is reversed within the chromosome.
- D. Duplication — Incorrect. A segment is present in an extra copy.
- E. Balanced translocation — Incorrect. Chromosome segments exchange positions without net gain or loss of genetic material, although reproductive risks may exist.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Deletion = loss.
- Duplication = extra copy.
- Inversion = segment reversed.
- Translocation = segment moved/exchanged between chromosomes.

questions.stem: Which description best characterizes a Robertsonian translocation?

options.label: A
options.text: Duplication of an entire mitochondrial genome

options.label: B
options.text: Gain of an entire extra chromosome set

options.label: C
options.text: Fusion of the long arms of two acrocentric chromosomes, with loss of their short arms

options.label: D
options.text: Reversal of a segment within one chromosome

questions.correctAnswerText: Fusion of the long arms of two acrocentric chromosomes, with loss of their short arms
questions.initialExplanation: Robertsonian translocation involves fusion of the long arms of two acrocentric chromosomes; a balanced carrier may be phenotypically normal but can have reproductive risks.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Mitochondrial duplication — Incorrect. This is not a Robertsonian rearrangement.

- B. Extra whole set — Incorrect. This describes polyploidy.
- C. Long-arm fusion — Correct. This is the defining mechanism of a Robertsonian translocation.
- D. Segment reversal — Incorrect. This describes an inversion.
- E. Nucleotide substitution — Incorrect. This is a sequence variant.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Robertsonian translocations involve acrocentric chromosomes.
- They are clinically important in some familial Down syndrome cases.
- Parental karyotyping and individualized genetic counselling are needed when translocation Down syndrome is identified.

## Mendelian Inheritance Patterns

questions.stem: Which pedigree pattern is typical of an autosomal dominant disorder with high penetrance?

options.label: A
options.text: males are affected and transmission is typically through the mother

options.label: B
options.text: The disorder appears when both parents are carriers

options.label: C
options.text: each affected father transmits the disorder to most sons

options.label: D
options.text: The disorder is transmitted exclusively through mitochondrial DNA

options.label: E
options.text: Vertical transmission, with affected individuals in successive generations

questions.correctAnswerText: Vertical transmission, with affected individuals in successive generations
questions.initialExplanation: Autosomal dominant conditions commonly affect successive generations because an affected heterozygous individual can transmit the pathogenic variant to approximately half of offspring.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Male-only maternal transmission — Incorrect. This suggests an X-linked or other sex-related pattern, not autosomal dominant inheritance.
- B. Both parents carriers — Incorrect. This is the classic risk setup for autosomal recessive disease.
- C. All sons from affected father — Incorrect. There is no father-to-son restriction or universal transmission in autosomal dominant inheritance.
- D. Mitochondrial only — Incorrect. Mitochondrial inheritance follows maternal transmission.

- E. Vertical transmission — Correct. Affected individuals often have an affected parent, although new mutations and reduced penetrance can complicate the pedigree.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Autosomal dominant: usually vertical pedigree.
- Males and females are affected.
- An affected heterozygous parent typically has a 50% chance of transmitting the variant to each child.

questions.stem: A heterozygous parent has an autosomal dominant disorder and the other parent is unaffected and non-carrier. What is the probability that each child will inherit the pathogenic variant?
questions.initialExplanation: Each pregnancy has an independent 1-in-2 chance of inheriting the variant from a heterozygous affected parent.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. 50% — Correct. Each child has a 50% chance of inheriting the variant.
- B. 75% — Incorrect. This is not the usual transmission risk in this parental combination.
- C. 100% — Incorrect. This would require every child to inherit the variant, which is not expected from a heterozygous parent.

- D. 0% — Incorrect. The affected heterozygous parent can transmit the variant.
- E. 25% — Incorrect. This is a typical risk for an affected child when both parents are carriers of an autosomal recessive condition.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Autosomal dominant heterozygous affected × unaffected non-carrier: 50% affected/inheriting variant per pregnancy.
- Each pregnancy is an independent event.
- Phenotype may vary because of variable expressivity and penetrance.

questions.stem: Which family pattern is most characteristic of autosomal recessive inheritance?

options.label: B
options.text: The condition is typically inherited from the maternal mitochondria

options.label: C
options.text: Affected children may be born to clinically unaffected carrier parents

options.label: D
options.text: An affected father transmits the condition to each daughter

options.label: E
options.text: An affected individual is typically present in each generation

questions.correctAnswerText: Affected children may be born to clinically unaffected carrier parents
questions.initialExplanation: Autosomal recessive disorders occur when a child inherits pathogenic variants in both copies of a gene; carrier parents are often clinically unaffected.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Males only — Incorrect. Autosomal recessive disorders affect males and females.
- B. Maternal mitochondria — Incorrect. This describes mitochondrial inheritance.

- C. Unaffected carrier parents — Correct. This explains why the disorder can appear to skip generations.
- D. All daughters — Incorrect. This pattern is not autosomal recessive.
- E. Every generation — Incorrect. This is more typical of autosomal dominant inheritance.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Autosomal recessive: often horizontal pattern among siblings.
- Consanguinity may increase the probability of both parents carrying the same rare variant.
- Both sexes are affected equally.

questions.stem: Both parents are heterozygous carriers of the same autosomal recessive disorder. What is the probability of an affected child in each pregnancy?
questions.initialExplanation: In a carrier-by-carrier cross, each pregnancy has a 25% chance of an affected child, 50% chance of a carrier child, and 25% chance of a child who inherited neither pathogenic variant.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. 25% — Correct. One of four possible genotype combinations is affected.
- B. 0% — Incorrect. Two carriers can have an affected child.
- C. 75% — Incorrect. This is the probability of a child who is not affected, assuming complete penetrance and the usual model.
- D. 50% — Incorrect. This is the probability of a carrier child.
- E. 100% — Incorrect. Not all children of carriers are affected.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- AR carrier × carrier: 25% affected, 50% carrier, 25% unaffected non-carrier.
- Risk is calculated for each pregnancy independently.
- Consanguinity can increase the chance of shared recessive variants.

questions.stem: Which statement is typical of an X-linked recessive disorder?

options.label: A
options.text: Father-to-son transmission is the defining feature

options.label: B
options.text: The disorder is inherited from the father

options.label: C
options.text: Affected males are common, while females may be unaffected carriers

options.label: D
options.text: Both sexes are typically affected equally

options.label: E
options.text: each daughter of a carrier mother are affected

questions.correctAnswerText: Affected males are common, while females may be unaffected carriers
questions.initialExplanation: Males have one X chromosome; a pathogenic variant on that X chromosome may cause disease, whereas females with one affected copy are often carriers.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Father-to-son transmission — Incorrect. Fathers transmit a Y chromosome, not their X chromosome, to sons.
- B. Father only — Incorrect. A son receives his X chromosome from his mother.

- C. Affected males and carrier females — Correct. This is the classic pattern for X-linked recessive disease.
- D. Equal sex distribution — Incorrect. Males are often more frequently affected.
- E. All daughters affected — Incorrect. Daughters of a carrier mother may be carriers or unaffected depending on the paternal genotype.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- X-linked recessive: usually affects males more often.
- No father-to-son transmission.
- Examples include hemophilia A/B, Duchenne muscular dystrophy, and G6PD deficiency.

questions.stem: A mother is a carrier of an X-linked recessive disorder and the father is unaffected. What is the risk for each son?
questions.correctAnswerText: 50% affected
questions.initialExplanation: Each son has a 50% chance of inheriting the maternal X chromosome carrying the variant and being affected.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. 50% affected — Correct. Each son receives his only X chromosome from the mother.
- B. 100% affected — Incorrect. The mother transmits either her normal or variant X chromosome.
- C. 50% carrier — Incorrect. Sons with the pathogenic X-linked recessive variant are generally affected rather than described as carriers.
- D. 25% affected — Incorrect. This would be the risk among all children in some ways of expressing the overall family risk, not among sons specifically.
- E. 100% unaffected — Incorrect. There is a 50% chance of inheriting the variant.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Carrier mother: 50% of sons affected; 50% of daughters carriers when father is unaffected.
- Each pregnancy is independent.
- A negative family history does not exclude a new mutation or previously unrecognized carrier status.

questions.stem: An affected male with an X-linked recessive disorder has children with an unaffected non-carrier woman. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The disorder is transmitted to children in routine care

options.label: C
options.text: each daughter are affected and most sons are carriers

options.label: D
options.text: each daughter inherit the affected X and are carriers; no sons inherit the father's X chromosome

options.label: E
options.text: Half of most sons inherit the affected X chromosome from their father

questions.correctAnswerText: each daughter inherit the affected X and are carriers; no sons inherit the father's X chromosome
questions.initialExplanation: An affected father transmits his X chromosome to all daughters and his Y chromosome to all sons. With an unaffected non-carrier mother, daughters are generally carriers and sons are unaffected.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Every child affected — Incorrect. The transmission pattern differs between sons and daughters.

- B. All sons affected — Incorrect. Sons receive the father's Y, not his X.
- C. Daughters affected — Incorrect. Daughters receive a normal X from the non-carrier mother and are usually carriers, not affected.
- D. Correct daughter/son pattern — Correct. This follows normal sex chromosome transmission.
- E. Half of sons inherit father's X — Incorrect. No son inherits the father's X chromosome.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- X-linked disorders: no father-to-son transmission.
- Affected father passes the variant X to all daughters.
- An affected daughter may occur in selected circumstances, e.g. affected father plus carrier/affected mother or monosomy X.

questions.stem: Which pedigree feature is characteristic of X-linked dominant inheritance?

options.label: A
options.text: The disorder is transmitted by mothers to sons

options.label: B
options.text: An affected father transmits the variant to each daughter and none of his sons

options.label: D
options.text: An affected father transmits the variant to most sons

options.label: E
options.text: Two carrier parents are typically required

questions.correctAnswerText: An affected father transmits the variant to each daughter and none of his sons
questions.initialExplanation: An affected male transmits his X chromosome to all daughters and his Y chromosome to all sons; in X-linked dominant disease, daughters who inherit the variant are affected.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Mothers to sons only — Incorrect. An affected mother can transmit the variant to sons or daughters.

- B. All daughters, no sons — Correct. This is the defining transmission pattern from an affected father.
- C. Males only — Incorrect. Females can also be affected.
- D. All sons — Incorrect. Sons receive the father's Y chromosome.
- E. Two carriers — Incorrect. This is not the usual X-linked dominant model.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- X-linked dominant: both sexes can be affected.
- Affected father: all daughters, no sons.
- Affected heterozygous mother: approximately 50% of sons and daughters inherit the variant.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes mitochondrial DNA inheritance?

options.label: A
options.text: An affected father transmits mitochondrial disease to most sons

options.label: B
options.text: It is located on the Y chromosome

options.label: C
options.text: It is usually maternally inherited because the zygote receives most cytoplasm and mitochondria from the ovum

options.label: D
options.text: It is inherited from the father

options.label: E
options.text: It follows the same 25% risk pattern as autosomal recessive disease

questions.correctAnswerText: It is usually maternally inherited because the zygote receives most cytoplasm and mitochondria from the ovum
questions.initialExplanation: Mitochondrial DNA is generally transmitted through the maternal line because mitochondria in the embryo are derived predominantly from the ovum.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Affected father to sons — Incorrect. Affected fathers do not usually transmit mitochondrial DNA disease.
- B. Y chromosome — Incorrect. Mitochondrial DNA is found in mitochondria, not on the Y chromosome.

- C. Maternal transmission — Correct. An affected mother may transmit mitochondrial variants to children of either sex, with variable expression.
- D. Paternal only — Incorrect. This is not the usual human mitochondrial inheritance pattern.
- E. Autosomal recessive ratio — Incorrect. Mitochondrial transmission and heteroplasmy produce a different risk pattern.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Mitochondrial inheritance is usually maternal.
- Both sons and daughters may be affected by an affected mother.
- An affected male generally does not transmit mitochondrial DNA disease to his children.

questions.stem: What does reduced penetrance mean in a genetic disorder?

options.label: A
options.text: The variant is typically absent from affected individuals

options.label: C
options.text: each carrier develops a more severe phenotype

options.label: D
options.text: Some individuals who carry a disease-associated genotype do not show the expected phenotype

questions.correctAnswerText: Some individuals who carry a disease-associated genotype do not show the expected phenotype
questions.initialExplanation: Penetrance is the proportion of individuals with a particular genotype who express the associated phenotype; reduced penetrance means not all carriers manifest the condition.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Variant absent — Incorrect. Reduced penetrance presupposes that the genotype is present.

- B. One sex only — Incorrect. Sex limitation is a different concept.
- C. More severe phenotype in all — Incorrect. This describes neither penetrance nor its reduction.
- D. Some carriers are unaffected — Correct. This explains why a pedigree may appear to skip a generation.
- E. Duplication — Incorrect. This is a structural chromosome abnormality.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Penetrance = whether the phenotype is expressed.
- Expressivity = degree or severity of phenotype among those who express it.
- Both can complicate pedigree interpretation.

## Multifactorial and Mitochondrial Inheritance; Genetic Counselling

topics.name: Multifactorial and Mitochondrial Inheritance; Genetic Counselling

questions.stem: Which mechanism best describes a multifactorial disorder?

options.label: A
options.text: A single mitochondrial variant transmitted by fathers

options.label: B
options.text: Interaction of multiple genetic variants with environmental factors

options.label: C
options.text: A disease caused exclusively by infection

options.label: D
options.text: A single chromosome trisomy in each case

options.label: E
options.text: A single autosomal recessive variant in homozygous form

questions.correctAnswerText: Interaction of multiple genetic variants with environmental factors
questions.initialExplanation: Multifactorial conditions result from the combined influence of multiple genes and environmental factors; recurrence risk is not usually described by a simple Mendelian ratio.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Paternal mitochondrial variant — Incorrect. Mitochondrial inheritance is generally maternal.
- B. Multiple genes and environment — Correct. This is the definition presented.
- C. Infection only — Incorrect. Infection is environmental but does not alone define multifactorial inheritance.

- D. Trisomy — Incorrect. This is a chromosomal disorder.
- E. One recessive gene — Incorrect. This is a single-gene autosomal recessive disorder.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Multifactorial: polygenic plus environmental contribution.
- Examples include neural tube defects, cleft lip/palate, congenital heart disease, and some common chronic diseases.
- Recurrence risk rises with more affected relatives and may rise with greater severity.

questions.stem: Which factor generally increases recurrence risk for a multifactorial condition within a family?

options.label: A
options.text: The presence of a normal karyotype in each family member

options.label: B
options.text: A greater number of affected close relatives

options.label: C
options.text: A distant unrelated individual with the condition

questions.correctAnswerText: A greater number of affected close relatives
questions.initialExplanation: The likelihood of recurrence for a multifactorial disorder generally increases when more close relatives are affected and may also increase with greater severity in the proband.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Normal karyotypes — Incorrect. A normal karyotype does not eliminate multifactorial risk.

- B. More affected close relatives — Correct. This suggests a greater familial genetic liability.
- C. Unrelated individual — Incorrect. This does not indicate increased inherited familial liability.
- D. Blood group — Incorrect. It is not a general predictor of multifactorial recurrence.
- E. Fewer affected relatives — Incorrect. This generally does not increase familial risk.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Multifactorial risk is empirical and family-specific.
- More affected first-degree relatives generally means higher recurrence risk.
- Avoid giving a simple 25% or 50% risk unless a Mendelian diagnosis has been established.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of genetic counselling?

options.label: A
options.text: To prescribe the same test to each family

options.label: B
options.text: To help individuals and families understand a genetic condition, inheritance, testing options, and reproductive or health implications

options.label: D
options.text: To guarantee that a genetic disorder will not usually recur

options.label: E
options.text: To replace clinical examination and laboratory diagnosis

questions.correctAnswerText: To help individuals and families understand a genetic condition, inheritance, testing options, and reproductive or health implications
questions.initialExplanation: Genetic counselling is a communication process that helps families understand the diagnosis, inheritance pattern, recurrence risk, available testing, and available support.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Same test for all — Incorrect. Testing should be selected according to the suspected condition and family context.

- B. Informed decision support — Correct. Counselling should be individualized, nondirective, and understandable.
- C. Choose sex — Incorrect. This is not the purpose of genetic counselling.
- D. Guarantee no recurrence — Incorrect. Counselling explains risk but cannot eliminate it.
- E. Replace diagnosis — Incorrect. Counselling complements diagnostic evaluation.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Genetic counselling is appropriate for congenital anomalies, developmental delay, infertility/recurrent pregnancy loss, ambiguous genitalia, consanguinity, and known familial disorders.
- Explain uncertainty and limitations of testing.
- Obtain informed consent and protect confidentiality.

questions.stem: Which family should be offered genetic counselling?

options.label: A
options.text: A child with a single episode of acute gastroenteritis

options.label: B
options.text: A family requesting routine antibiotics for a cold

options.label: C
options.text: A child with one uncomplicated episode of viral rhinitis

options.label: D
options.text: A couple with recurrent pregnancy loss and a previous child with a suspected chromosomal disorder

options.label: E
options.text: A healthy child with a minor superficial abrasion

questions.correctAnswerText: A couple with recurrent pregnancy loss and a previous child with a suspected chromosomal disorder
questions.initialExplanation: Recurrent pregnancy loss, congenital anomalies, developmental delay, known familial genetic disorders, and parental chromosome rearrangements are indications for genetics assessment.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Acute gastroenteritis — Incorrect. This is usually an acute infectious condition.
- B. Antibiotics for a cold — Incorrect. This is not a reason for genetic counselling.

- C. Viral rhinitis — Incorrect. This is not a genetics indication.
- D. Recurrent loss and affected child — Correct. These findings may indicate an inherited or chromosomal cause and affect recurrence risk.
- E. Minor abrasion — Incorrect. This does not suggest a hereditary disorder.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Consider counselling for congenital malformations, infertility, recurrent miscarriage, developmental delay, consanguinity, and advanced parental age when relevant.
- Review the three-generation family history when indicated.
- Testing and recurrence counselling depend on the confirmed diagnosis.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of drawing a family pedigree during genetic assessment?

options.label: B
options.text: To map affected and unaffected relatives and identify possible inheritance patterns across generations

options.label: C
options.text: To measure the child's growth velocity

options.label: D
options.text: To diagnose a congenital heart defect

questions.correctAnswerText: To map affected and unaffected relatives and identify possible inheritance patterns across generations
questions.initialExplanation: A pedigree organizes family history and can reveal vertical, horizontal, sex-linked, or maternal transmission patterns.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Replace karyotype — Incorrect. Pedigree analysis guides testing but cannot replace laboratory confirmation.

- B. Family pattern — Correct. Pedigrees help identify relatives at risk and guide testing.
- C. Growth velocity — Incorrect. This is measured using serial anthropometry.
- D. Heart defect — Incorrect. This requires clinical examination and cardiac investigations.
- E. Enzyme concentration — Incorrect. This requires laboratory testing.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Pedigrees use standard symbols for sex, affected status, relationships, and generations.
- Roman numerals usually identify generations; Arabic numerals identify individuals within a generation.
- Include relevant family history from both maternal and paternal sides.

## Down Syndrome

questions.stem: Down syndrome is most commonly caused by which chromosomal abnormality?
questions.correctAnswerText: Trisomy 21
questions.initialExplanation: Down syndrome is most commonly caused by an extra copy of chromosome 21.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. 47,XXY — Incorrect. This is Klinefelter syndrome.

- B. Trisomy 21 — Correct. This is the common chromosomal mechanism of Down syndrome.
- C. Trisomy 18 — Incorrect. This causes Edwards syndrome.
- D. Trisomy 13 — Incorrect. This causes Patau syndrome.
- E. Monosomy X — Incorrect. This is the classic Turner syndrome karyotype.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Down syndrome: trisomy 21.
- The additional chromosome may arise from meiotic nondisjunction, translocation, or mosaicism.
- Karyotyping confirms the chromosomal diagnosis and identifies the mechanism.

questions.stem: Which mechanism accounts for the majority of cases of Down syndrome?

options.label: C
options.text: Meiotic nondisjunction resulting in an extra chromosome 21

options.label: E
options.text: Deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5

questions.correctAnswerText: Meiotic nondisjunction resulting in an extra chromosome 21
questions.initialExplanation: Most cases of Down syndrome result from meiotic nondisjunction, producing a child with free trisomy 21.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Paternal 15q deletion — Incorrect. This is associated with Prader-Willi syndrome.

- B. Monosomy X — Incorrect. This causes Turner syndrome.
- C. Meiotic nondisjunction — Correct. Failure of chromosome separation during meiosis produces an extra chromosome 21.
- D. FMR1 mutation — Incorrect. This causes Fragile X syndrome.
- E. Deletion 5p — Incorrect. This causes cri-du-chat syndrome.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Most Down syndrome: free trisomy 21 from nondisjunction.
- Translocation and mosaic forms are less common.
- Recurrence counselling depends on the precise cytogenetic mechanism and parental karyotypes.

questions.stem: A child has a Robertsonian translocation involving chromosome 21. Which additional investigation is important for recurrence counselling?
questions.correctAnswerText: Karyotyping of both parents
questions.initialExplanation: Parental karyotyping is important when a child has translocation Down syndrome because one parent may carry a balanced Robertsonian translocation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Sweat test — Incorrect. This assesses cystic fibrosis, not a chromosome rearrangement.

- B. Parental karyotypes — Correct. A balanced carrier parent may be phenotypically normal but have an increased risk of unbalanced pregnancies.
- C. Echocardiography — Incorrect. Cardiac assessment is important for the child, but it does not determine translocation recurrence.
- D. Calcium — Incorrect. This does not identify a chromosome rearrangement.
- E. Urine culture — Incorrect. This is unrelated.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Translocation Down syndrome: determine whether a parent is a balanced carrier.
- Recurrence risk differs according to the chromosomes involved and which parent carries the rearrangement.
- Do not quote one universal recurrence percentage without the parental karyotype.

questions.stem: Which combination is characteristic of Down syndrome?

options.label: A
options.text: Webbed neck, shield chest, and streak ovaries

options.label: B
options.text: Polydactyly, cleft lip, and cutis aplasia

options.label: C
options.text: Long limbs, arachnodactyly, and ectopia lentis

options.label: D
options.text: Up-slanting palpebral fissures, epicanthic folds, hypotonia, and single transverse palmar crease

options.label: E
options.text: Macroorchidism, long face, and large ears

questions.correctAnswerText: Up-slanting palpebral fissures, epicanthic folds, hypotonia, and single transverse palmar crease
questions.initialExplanation: Down syndrome has a recognizable pattern of craniofacial, hand, and tone findings, although expression varies between individuals.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Turner features — Incorrect. Webbed neck, shield chest, and gonadal dysgenesis suggest Turner syndrome.
- B. Patau features — Incorrect. Polydactyly, cleft lip/palate, and scalp defects suggest trisomy 13.
- C. Marfan features — Incorrect. Long limbs, arachnodactyly, and ectopia lentis suggest Marfan syndrome.
- D. Down phenotype — Correct. These are classic physical features.
- E. Fragile X features — Incorrect. Macroorchidism, long face, and prominent ears are associated with Fragile X syndrome.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Down syndrome: hypotonia, characteristic facial appearance, single palmar crease, sandal gap.
- Physical features vary; clinical appearance alone does not determine severity.
- Confirm the diagnosis with chromosome analysis.

questions.stem: Which congenital heart defect is classically associated with Down syndrome and is highlighted?
questions.correctAnswerText: Atrioventricular septal defect (AVSD)
questions.initialExplanation: AVSD, also called an endocardial cushion defect, is strongly associated with Down syndrome.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Isolated pulmonary stenosis — Incorrect. This is more associated with Noonan syndrome.

- B. Coarctation — Incorrect. This is more classically associated with Turner syndrome.
- C. Tetralogy of Fallot — Incorrect. It can occur in congenital syndromes but is not the classic association highlighted here.
- D. AVSD — Correct. This is the classic cardiac association emphasized.
- E. Transposition — Incorrect. This is not the classic Down syndrome association.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- A child with Down syndrome requires cardiac assessment, including echocardiography according to the clinical pathway.
- AVSD is a major association.
- Early recognition of congenital heart disease is important.

questions.stem: Which gastrointestinal anomaly is classically associated with Down syndrome?
questions.correctAnswerText: Duodenal atresia
questions.initialExplanation: Duodenal atresia is a well-known gastrointestinal association of Down syndrome; Hirschsprung disease and celiac disease are also increased.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Pyloric stenosis — Incorrect. This is not the classic Down syndrome association.
- B. Biliary atresia — Incorrect. It is not present in every child and is not the classic GI association.
- C. Duodenal atresia — Correct. It is a classic association and may present with neonatal vomiting.
- D. Hirschsprung impossible — Incorrect. Hirschsprung disease is associated with Down syndrome.
- E. Meckel only — Incorrect. This is not the characteristic association.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Down syndrome: duodenal atresia, Hirschsprung disease, celiac disease, reflux, and feeding/growth problems.
- Consider GI obstruction in a newborn with bilious vomiting.
- Evaluate persistent constipation and poor growth appropriately.

questions.stem: Which conditions require ongoing surveillance in children with Down syndrome?

options.label: C
options.text: Thyroid dysfunction, hearing and vision problems, celiac disease, and sleep apnea

options.label: D
options.text: iron deficiency in children in routine care

questions.correctAnswerText: Thyroid dysfunction, hearing and vision problems, celiac disease, and sleep apnea
questions.initialExplanation: Down syndrome is associated with multiple health conditions that require anticipatory guidance and periodic assessment.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Appendicitis — Incorrect. This is not the specific surveillance package.
- B. No surveillance — Incorrect. Ongoing monitoring is essential.
- C. Multisystem surveillance — Correct. Key features include thyroid disease, hearing/vision impairment, celiac disease, and sleep apnea.
- D. Iron deficiency only — Incorrect. Nutritional assessment is important, but the surveillance needs are broader.
- E. Renal stones only — Incorrect. This does not cover the major associated conditions.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Screen/monitor thyroid function, hearing, vision, sleep-disordered breathing, and celiac disease according to current guidance.
- Assess growth using appropriate Down syndrome growth references where available.
- Monitor development and provide multidisciplinary support.

questions.stem: Which test confirms a diagnosis of Down syndrome after birth?
questions.correctAnswerText: Chromosome analysis (karyotype)
questions.initialExplanation: Screening tests estimate the probability of Down syndrome; diagnostic chromosome analysis confirms the chromosomal abnormality and distinguishes free trisomy, translocation, and mosaicism.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Nuchal translucency — Incorrect. This is a prenatal screening marker.
- B. CBC — Incorrect. Blood counts may show associated findings but do not confirm trisomy 21.

- C. Triple test — Incorrect. This is a prenatal screening test, not a diagnostic confirmation.
- D. Karyotype — Correct. It confirms the chromosomal constitution.
- E. Echocardiography — Incorrect. This assesses cardiac anomalies, not chromosome number.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Screening estimates risk; diagnostic testing confirms.
- Postnatal karyotyping identifies the mechanism of trisomy 21.
- A translocation result changes parental testing and recurrence counselling.

## Trisomy 18, Trisomy 13, Turner, and Noonan Syndromes

topics.name: Trisomy 18, Trisomy 13, Turner, and Noonan Syndromes

questions.stem: Edwards syndrome is caused by which chromosomal abnormality?
questions.correctAnswerText: Trisomy 18
questions.initialExplanation: Edwards syndrome is trisomy 18 and is associated with growth restriction, characteristic hand and foot abnormalities, and multiple congenital anomalies.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Trisomy 21 — Incorrect. This causes Down syndrome.
- B. Monosomy X — Incorrect. This causes Turner syndrome.
- C. Trisomy 13 — Incorrect. This causes Patau syndrome.
- D. 47,XXY — Incorrect. This causes Klinefelter syndrome.

- E. Trisomy 18 — Correct. This is the chromosomal basis of Edwards syndrome.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Edwards = trisomy 18.
- Features include prominent occiput, micrognathia, clenched/overlapping fingers, rocker-bottom feet, and congenital heart disease.
- Severe multisystem disease is common.

questions.stem: Which physical finding is particularly characteristic of Patau syndrome (trisomy 13)?

options.label: B
options.text: Single transverse palmar crease and sandal gap

options.label: D
options.text: Postaxial polydactyly with cleft lip/palate and scalp defects

options.label: E
options.text: Shield chest and widely spaced nipples

questions.correctAnswerText: Postaxial polydactyly with cleft lip/palate and scalp defects
questions.initialExplanation: Patau syndrome is associated with trisomy 13 and may cause severe midline defects, cleft lip/palate, polydactyly, microphthalmia, and cutis aplasia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Marfan features — Incorrect. These suggest Marfan syndrome.
- B. Down features — Incorrect. These are associated with trisomy 21.
- C. Fragile X features — Incorrect. These suggest Fragile X syndrome.

- D. Patau features — Correct. These are characteristic associations.
- E. Turner features — Incorrect. Shield chest and widely spaced nipples are typical of Turner syndrome.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Patau = trisomy 13.
- Look for polydactyly, cleft lip/palate, scalp defects, microphthalmia, and severe congenital anomalies.
- Prognosis is often poor because of severe multisystem involvement.

questions.stem: Which feature most strongly favors Edwards syndrome over Patau syndrome?

options.label: E
options.text: Clenched hands with overlapping fingers and rocker-bottom feet

questions.correctAnswerText: Clenched hands with overlapping fingers and rocker-bottom feet
questions.initialExplanation: Edwards syndrome classically causes clenched fists with overlapping fingers and rocker-bottom feet; Patau syndrome is more associated with polydactyly and midline defects.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Polydactyly and cleft lip/palate — Incorrect. These favor Patau syndrome.
- B. Cleft palate and scalp defects — Incorrect. These are associated with Patau syndrome.

- C. Omphalocele and polydactyly — Incorrect. This combination favors Patau syndrome.
- D. Cutis aplasia and microphthalmia — Incorrect. These are associated with Patau syndrome.
- E. Overlapping fingers/rocker-bottom feet — Correct. This is a classic Edwards pattern.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Edwards (18): overlapping fingers, prominent occiput, rocker-bottom feet.
- Patau (13): polydactyly, cleft lip/palate, microphthalmia, cutis aplasia.
- Both are severe trisomy syndromes with congenital heart disease.

questions.stem: What is the classic karyotype in Turner syndrome?
questions.initialExplanation: Turner syndrome classically results from complete or partial absence of one X chromosome; mosaic and structural variants also occur.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Trisomy 21 — Incorrect. This is Down syndrome.
- B. 47,XXY — Incorrect. This is Klinefelter syndrome.
- C. 46,XX — Incorrect. This is a typical female karyotype, although phenotypic conditions can occur with other genetic mechanisms.

- D. 45,X — Correct. This is the classic monosomy X karyotype.
- E. Trisomy 13 — Incorrect. This is Patau syndrome.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Turner syndrome: 45,X or mosaic/structural X abnormalities.
- Phenotype includes short stature, gonadal dysgenesis, and possible congenital heart and renal anomalies.
- Confirm with chromosome analysis.

questions.stem: A newborn girl has swelling of the hands and feet due to lymphedema and a webbed neck. Which diagnosis should be considered?
questions.correctAnswerText: Turner syndrome
questions.initialExplanation: Congenital lymphedema of the hands and feet and webbed neck are classic neonatal clues to Turner syndrome.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Down syndrome — Incorrect. Down syndrome has a different characteristic phenotype.
- B. Marfan — Incorrect. Marfan syndrome is characterized by tall stature and connective tissue findings.

- C. Klinefelter — Incorrect. This affects males and is associated with 47,XXY.
- D. Noonan syndrome — Incorrect. It can resemble Turner syndrome but affects both sexes and has a normal karyotype; it does not classically present with congenital lymphedema as its defining feature.
- E. Turner syndrome — Correct. This phenotype should prompt karyotyping.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Neonatal lymphedema and webbed neck suggest Turner syndrome.
- Consider cystic hygroma antenatally.
- Karyotype confirms the diagnosis.

questions.stem: Which cardiovascular abnormality is classically associated with Turner syndrome?

options.label: A
options.text: Complete transposition of the great arteries

questions.correctAnswerText: Coarctation of the aorta
questions.initialExplanation: Turner syndrome is associated with left-sided cardiac lesions, particularly coarctation of the aorta and bicuspid aortic valve.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Transposition — Incorrect. This is not the typical Turner association.
- B. Ebstein anomaly — Incorrect. This is not the classic Turner lesion.

- C. AVSD — Incorrect. This is strongly associated with Down syndrome.
- D. Coarctation — Correct. This is a classic Turner syndrome association.
- E. PDA only — Incorrect. PDA may occur in many settings but is not the classic Turner lesion.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Turner: coarctation and bicuspid aortic valve.
- Renal anomalies include horseshoe kidney.
- Echocardiography and renal imaging are part of clinical evaluation.

questions.stem: Which endocrine laboratory pattern is expected in ovarian failure due to Turner syndrome?

options.label: B
options.text: Increased FSH and LH with low estrogen

options.label: C
options.text: Low FSH and LH with high estrogen

options.label: D
options.text: Normal gonadotropins with severe androgen excess

questions.correctAnswerText: Increased FSH and LH with low estrogen
questions.initialExplanation: Gonadal dysgenesis leads to ovarian insufficiency, low estrogen, and elevated gonadotropins due to loss of negative feedback.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. High testosterone — Incorrect. This is not the typical Turner pattern.
- B. High FSH/LH, low estrogen — Correct. This is hypergonadotropic hypogonadism.
- C. Low FSH/LH, high estrogen — Incorrect. This suggests central suppression rather than ovarian failure.
- D. Androgen excess — Incorrect. This does not describe ovarian dysgenesis.

- E. Prolactin — Incorrect. Hyperprolactinemia is not the defining endocrine finding.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Turner: ovarian dysgenesis and hypergonadotropic hypogonadism.
- Short stature is a cardinal feature.
- Management may include growth hormone and estrogen replacement under specialist care.

questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes Noonan syndrome from Turner syndrome?

options.label: A
options.text: Noonan syndrome is a mitochondrial disorder

options.label: B
options.text: Noonan syndrome affects males and females and usually has a normal karyotype

options.label: C
options.text: Noonan syndrome is caused by trisomy 21

options.label: D
options.text: Noonan syndrome affects females and is caused by 45,X

questions.correctAnswerText: Noonan syndrome affects males and females and usually has a normal karyotype
questions.initialExplanation: Noonan syndrome is usually an autosomal dominant RASopathy; it can resemble Turner syndrome phenotypically but occurs in both sexes and does not typically involve monosomy X.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Mitochondrial disorder — Incorrect. It is generally associated with variants in RAS-MAPK pathway genes.
- B. Both sexes, normal karyotype — Correct. This is a key distinction from Turner syndrome.
- C. Trisomy 21 — Incorrect. This causes Down syndrome.

- D. Female-only 45,X — Incorrect. This describes Turner syndrome.
- E. Always infertile — Incorrect. Fertility may be normal, although cryptorchidism can affect male reproductive function.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Noonan: affects both sexes, often autosomal dominant, normal chromosome number.
- Phenotypic overlap with Turner syndrome.
- Cardiac associations include pulmonary valve stenosis and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

questions.stem: Which cardiac lesion is particularly associated with Noonan syndrome?
questions.correctAnswerText: Pulmonary valve stenosis
questions.initialExplanation: Pulmonary valve stenosis is a classic cardiac lesion in Noonan syndrome; hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is another important association.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. AVSD — Incorrect. This is classically associated with Down syndrome.
- B. Coarctation — Incorrect. This is classically associated with Turner syndrome.
- C. Pulmonary stenosis — Correct. This is the cardiac lesion highlighted.
- D. Hypoplastic left heart — Incorrect. It is not the typical Noonan association.
- E. TAPVR — Incorrect. It is not the classic lesion in Noonan syndrome.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Noonan: pulmonary stenosis and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
- Short/webbed neck, characteristic facies, short stature.
- Evaluate for bleeding tendency and cryptorchidism in males.

## Fragile X, Angelman, Prader-Willi, and Beckwith-Wiedemann

topics.name: Fragile X, Angelman, Prader-Willi, and Beckwith-Wiedemann

questions.stem: Fragile X syndrome is most commonly associated with a pathogenic expansion in which gene?
questions.correctAnswerText: FMR1
questions.initialExplanation: Fragile X syndrome is caused by a CGG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the FMR1 gene on the X chromosome, leading to reduced or absent FMRP expression in the full mutation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. FBN1 — Incorrect. Pathogenic variants cause Marfan syndrome.
- B. ATP7B — Incorrect. Pathogenic variants cause Wilson disease.
- C. FMR1 — Correct. This gene is responsible for Fragile X syndrome.
- D. DMD — Incorrect. Pathogenic variants cause Duchenne/Becker muscular dystrophy.

- E. CFTR — Incorrect. Pathogenic variants cause cystic fibrosis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Fragile X: CGG repeat expansion in FMR1.
- It is an X-linked condition and a common inherited cause of intellectual disability.
- Anticipation can occur because repeat expansion risk differs by maternal transmission.

questions.stem: Which combination of features is characteristic of Fragile X syndrome, particularly after puberty?

options.label: A
options.text: Webbed neck, shield chest, and lymphedema

options.label: B
options.text: Polydactyly, cleft palate, and cutis aplasia

options.label: C
options.text: Tall stature, arachnodactyly, and ectopia lentis

options.label: D
options.text: Long face, large prominent ears, and macroorchidism

questions.correctAnswerText: Long face, large prominent ears, and macroorchidism
questions.initialExplanation: Fragile X may present with learning difficulties, characteristic facial features, and macroorchidism after puberty.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Turner phenotype — Incorrect. These are features of Turner syndrome.
- B. Patau phenotype — Incorrect. These suggest trisomy 13.
- C. Marfan phenotype — Incorrect. These are connective tissue features.
- D. Fragile X phenotype — Correct. These are classical features described.
- E. Beckwith-Wiedemann phenotype — Incorrect. These features suggest an overgrowth syndrome.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Fragile X: intellectual/learning difficulties, long face, large ears, macroorchidism.
- Joint laxity, scoliosis, mitral valve prolapse, autism, or hyperactivity may coexist.
- Macroorchidism is more obvious after puberty.

questions.stem: Which clinical combination is characteristic of Angelman syndrome?

options.label: A
options.text: Tall stature, ectopia lentis, and aortic root dilation

options.label: B
options.text: Severe developmental impairment, seizures, markedly limited speech, and a happy/excitable demeanor with frequent laughter

options.label: C
options.text: Polydactyly with cleft lip and palate

options.label: D
options.text: Severe obesity beginning in infancy with hyperphagia

questions.correctAnswerText: Severe developmental impairment, seizures, markedly limited speech, and a happy/excitable demeanor with frequent laughter
questions.initialExplanation: Angelman syndrome is associated with severe developmental delay, speech impairment, seizures, hypotonia/ataxia, and a characteristic happy disposition.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Marfan syndrome — Incorrect. This is a connective-tissue disorder.
- B. Angelman syndrome — Correct. This is the classic clinical profile.
- C. Patau syndrome — Incorrect. This causes trisomy 13 features.

- D. Prader-Willi syndrome — Incorrect. Hyperphagia and obesity are characteristic of Prader-Willi, not the defining Angelman presentation.
- E. Turner syndrome — Incorrect. This causes ovarian dysgenesis and short stature.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Angelman: severe developmental delay, absent/limited speech, seizures, ataxia, frequent laughter.
- It often involves loss of maternal UBE3A expression in the brain.
- Prader-Willi and Angelman are imprinting disorders involving chromosome 15q11-q13 but have different parent-of-origin mechanisms.

questions.stem: Prader-Willi syndrome is classically associated with loss of expression of which parental contribution at chromosome 15q11-q13?
questions.correctAnswerText: Paternal contribution
questions.initialExplanation: Prader-Willi syndrome results from absent expression of paternally derived genes in the 15q11-q13 region, due to deletion, maternal uniparental disomy, or an imprinting defect.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Chromosome 21 — Incorrect. This is unrelated to Prader-Willi syndrome.
- B. Paternal contribution — Correct. Loss of paternal expression produces Prader-Willi syndrome.
- C. Maternal contribution — Incorrect. Loss of maternal UBE3A expression in relevant brain tissue is associated with Angelman syndrome.
- D. X chromosome — Incorrect. The syndrome involves chromosome 15.
- E. Mitochondrial DNA — Incorrect. This is not a mitochondrial disorder.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Prader-Willi: absence of paternal gene expression at 15q11-q13.
- Angelman: loss of maternal UBE3A expression in the brain.
- Parent-of-origin effect is central to understanding both disorders.

questions.stem: Which sequence best describes the typical evolution of Prader-Willi syndrome?

options.label: A
options.text: Macroglossia at birth followed by hypoglycemia and macrosomia

options.label: B
options.text: Neonatal hyperphagia followed by spontaneous complete resolution

options.label: C
options.text: Neonatal hypotonia and poor feeding, followed later by hyperphagia and obesity risk

options.label: D
options.text: Tall stature and aortic dissection in adolescence

options.label: E
options.text: Severe lymphedema at birth followed by ovarian failure

questions.correctAnswerText: Neonatal hypotonia and poor feeding, followed later by hyperphagia and obesity risk
questions.initialExplanation: Infants with Prader-Willi syndrome commonly have marked hypotonia and feeding difficulties; later childhood is associated with hyperphagia, obesity risk, short stature, and hypogonadism.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Beckwith-Wiedemann — Incorrect. Macroglossia, macrosomia, and neonatal hypoglycemia suggest Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome.
- B. Hyperphagia at birth — Incorrect. Early infancy is usually characterized by hypotonia and feeding difficulty.
- C. Biphasic feeding pattern — Correct. Early poor feeding transitions to later hyperphagia in many children.
- D. Marfan — Incorrect. Tall stature and aortic disease suggest Marfan syndrome.

- E. Turner — Incorrect. Lymphedema and ovarian failure suggest Turner syndrome.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Prader-Willi: neonatal hypotonia/poor feeding; later hyperphagia and obesity risk.
- Other features include hypogonadism, small hands/feet, short stature, and developmental difficulty.
- Early nutritional and endocrine management is important.

questions.stem: Which combination is most characteristic of Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome?

options.label: A
options.text: Hypotonia at birth followed by hyperphagia in childhood

options.label: C
options.text: Short stature, webbed neck, and ovarian failure

options.label: D
options.text: Long limbs, arachnodactyly, and ectopia lentis

options.label: E
options.text: Macrosomia, macroglossia, abdominal wall defect, and neonatal hypoglycemia

questions.correctAnswerText: Macrosomia, macroglossia, abdominal wall defect, and neonatal hypoglycemia
questions.initialExplanation: Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome is an overgrowth/imprinting disorder characterized by macrosomia, macroglossia, visceromegaly, abdominal wall defects, and hyperinsulinemic neonatal hypoglycemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Prader-Willi — Incorrect. This describes the characteristic feeding evolution in Prader-Willi syndrome.

- B. Patau — Incorrect. These suggest trisomy 13.
- C. Turner — Incorrect. These are Turner syndrome features.
- D. Marfan — Incorrect. These are connective-tissue features.
- E. Beckwith-Wiedemann — Correct. This matches the characteristic overgrowth phenotype.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Beckwith-Wiedemann: macrosomia, macroglossia, omphalocele/umbilical wall defect, visceromegaly, neonatal hypoglycemia.
- Tumor predisposition includes Wilms tumor and hepatoblastoma.
- Requires syndrome-specific tumor surveillance through specialist protocols.

questions.stem: Which pediatric tumor is an important association requiring surveillance in Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome?

options.label: B
options.text: Retinoblastoma in children in routine care

questions.correctAnswerText: Wilms tumor
questions.initialExplanation: Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome increases the risk of embryonal tumors, particularly Wilms tumor and hepatoblastoma; surveillance is tailored to the molecular subtype and local protocol.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Medulloblastoma — Incorrect. This is not the characteristic tumor risk.
- B. Retinoblastoma — Incorrect. Retinoblastoma is associated with RB1 variants, not classically Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome.
- C. Osteosarcoma — Incorrect. This is not the principal association.
- D. Rhabdomyosarcoma — Incorrect. This is not the classic tumor association in this syndrome.

- E. Wilms tumor — Correct. This is a key tumor association.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Beckwith-Wiedemann: embryonal tumor predisposition.
- Wilms tumor and hepatoblastoma are important.
- Surveillance should follow current specialist guidance; do not use a one-size-fits-all schedule.

## Marfan, Klinefelter, Alagille, Williams, and DiGeorge Syndromes

topics.name: Marfan, Klinefelter, Alagille, Williams, and DiGeorge Syndromes

questions.stem: Marfan syndrome is most commonly caused by pathogenic variants in which gene?
questions.correctAnswerText: FBN1
questions.initialExplanation: Marfan syndrome is an autosomal dominant connective-tissue disorder commonly caused by variants in FBN1, which encodes fibrillin-1.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. CFTR — Incorrect. This causes cystic fibrosis.
- B. UBE3A — Incorrect. This is associated with Angelman syndrome.

- C. FMR1 — Incorrect. This causes Fragile X syndrome.
- D. ATP7B — Incorrect. This causes Wilson disease.
- E. FBN1 — Correct. This gene is central to Marfan syndrome.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Marfan: usually autosomal dominant.
- FBN1 encodes fibrillin-1.
- A proportion of cases arise from de novo variants.

questions.stem: Which combination is characteristic of Marfan syndrome?

options.label: A
options.text: Macroorchidism, long face, and large ears

options.label: B
options.text: Short stature, macroglossia, and neonatal hypoglycemia

options.label: C
options.text: Tall stature, arachnodactyly, positive thumb/wrist signs, and ectopia lentis

options.label: D
options.text: Webbed neck, lymphedema, and ovarian dysgenesis

options.label: E
options.text: Polydactyly, cleft palate, and scalp defects

questions.correctAnswerText: Tall stature, arachnodactyly, positive thumb/wrist signs, and ectopia lentis
questions.initialExplanation: Marfan syndrome is a connective-tissue disorder with skeletal, ocular, cardiovascular, and sometimes pulmonary manifestations.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Fragile X — Incorrect. These are Fragile X features.

- B. Beckwith-Wiedemann — Incorrect. These are overgrowth syndrome features.
- C. Marfan phenotype — Correct. These are classic findings.
- D. Turner — Incorrect. These are Turner syndrome features.
- E. Patau — Incorrect. These are trisomy 13 features.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Marfan: tall stature, long limbs, arachnodactyly, pectus deformity, scoliosis, ectopia lentis.
- Cardiovascular risk includes aortic root dilation and dissection.
- Requires cardiovascular and ophthalmological assessment.

questions.stem: Which cardiovascular complication is most important to monitor in Marfan syndrome?

options.label: B
options.text: Aortic root dilation with risk of aortic dissection

options.label: C
options.text: Complete heart block in each patient

questions.correctAnswerText: Aortic root dilation with risk of aortic dissection
questions.initialExplanation: Fibrillin-1 abnormalities weaken connective tissue in the aortic wall, predisposing to aortic root dilation and potentially life-threatening dissection.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Coarctation — Incorrect. This is more associated with Turner syndrome.
- B. Aortic root disease — Correct. This is the major life-threatening cardiovascular concern.
- C. Complete heart block — Incorrect. This is not the defining Marfan complication.

- D. Pulmonary stenosis — Incorrect. This is associated with Noonan syndrome.
- E. AVSD — Incorrect. This is associated with Down syndrome.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Regular echocardiographic surveillance is important.
- Avoid high-risk activities according to specialist advice.
- Early recognition of aortic disease reduces risk of catastrophic complications.

questions.stem: Which karyotype is typical of Klinefelter syndrome?
questions.correctAnswerText: 47,XXY
questions.initialExplanation: Klinefelter syndrome is a sex chromosome aneuploidy affecting males, classically with an additional X chromosome.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. 45,X — Incorrect. This is Turner syndrome.
- B. Trisomy 13 — Incorrect. This is Patau syndrome.
- C. Trisomy 21 — Incorrect. This is Down syndrome.
- D. 46,XY — Incorrect. This is a typical male karyotype.

- E. 47,XXY — Correct. This is the classic Klinefelter karyotype.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Klinefelter: 47,XXY.
- Typical features include small testes, hypergonadotropic hypogonadism, tall stature, gynecomastia, and infertility.
- Intelligence is often within the normal range, although language/learning difficulties may occur.

questions.stem: Which hormonal pattern is expected in primary testicular failure in Klinefelter syndrome?

options.label: A
options.text: Low testosterone with increased LH and FSH

options.label: C
options.text: High testosterone with suppressed LH and FSH

options.label: D
options.text: Low LH and FSH with high testosterone

options.label: E
options.text: Normal gonadotropins with severe androgen excess

questions.correctAnswerText: Low testosterone with increased LH and FSH
questions.initialExplanation: Testicular failure reduces testosterone and inhibin feedback, causing increased gonadotropins (hypergonadotropic hypogonadism).
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Low testosterone, high LH/FSH — Correct. This is the expected primary gonadal failure pattern.
- B. Isolated estrogen pattern — Incorrect. This does not describe primary testicular failure.
- C. High testosterone — Incorrect. This is not the expected finding.
- D. Low gonadotropins — Incorrect. This suggests central hypogonadism.
- E. Androgen excess — Incorrect. Klinefelter syndrome involves testicular insufficiency, not androgen excess.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Small testes and infertility are important clues.
- Testosterone may be low with elevated LH/FSH.
- Karyotyping confirms the diagnosis.

questions.stem: Which combination is characteristic of Alagille syndrome?

options.label: D
options.text: Aortic root dilation, arachnodactyly, and ectopia lentis

options.label: E
options.text: Cholestasis from paucity of intrahepatic bile ducts, peripheral pulmonary stenosis, and characteristic facies

questions.correctAnswerText: Cholestasis from paucity of intrahepatic bile ducts, peripheral pulmonary stenosis, and characteristic facies
questions.initialExplanation: Alagille syndrome is a multisystem disorder commonly associated with bile duct paucity, cholestatic liver disease, cardiac abnormalities, characteristic facial features, vertebral changes, and ocular findings.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Beckwith-Wiedemann — Incorrect. This is an overgrowth syndrome.
- B. Prader-Willi — Incorrect. This is an imprinting disorder with a characteristic feeding evolution.
- C. Patau — Incorrect. This is trisomy 13.

- D. Marfan — Incorrect. This is a connective-tissue disorder.
- E. Alagille syndrome — Correct. This is the classic multisystem pattern.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Alagille: bile duct paucity and cholestasis.
- Cardiac association: peripheral pulmonary artery stenosis.
- Other features include triangular facies, posterior embryotoxon, and butterfly vertebrae.

questions.stem: Which combination is typical of Williams syndrome?

options.label: A
options.text: Polydactyly, cleft palate, and cutis aplasia

options.label: B
options.text: Webbed neck, lymphedema, and ovarian failure

options.label: C
options.text: Aortic root dilation with ectopia lentis

options.label: E
options.text: Elfin-like facial appearance, supravalvular aortic stenosis, and a characteristic social/cognitive profile

questions.correctAnswerText: Elfin-like facial appearance, supravalvular aortic stenosis, and a characteristic social/cognitive profile
questions.initialExplanation: Williams syndrome is usually caused by a 7q11.23 microdeletion that includes ELN, leading to supravalvular aortic stenosis and a recognizable neurodevelopmental profile.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Patau — Incorrect. These are trisomy 13 features.
- B. Turner syndrome — Incorrect. These are Turner features.
- C. Marfan — Incorrect. These are Marfan features.

- D. Fragile X — Incorrect. These are Fragile X features.
- E. Williams syndrome — Correct. This is the key triad highlighted.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Williams: 7q11.23 microdeletion.
- Supravalvular aortic stenosis and transient hypercalcemia may occur.
- Molecular confirmation may use microarray or an appropriate targeted test.

questions.stem: DiGeorge syndrome is classically associated with which chromosomal deletion?
questions.correctAnswerText: 22q11.2 deletion
questions.initialExplanation: DiGeorge syndrome is commonly associated with a 22q11.2 deletion that disrupts development of the pharyngeal pouch derivatives.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. 21q duplication — Incorrect. This is not the classic cause of DiGeorge syndrome.

- B. 7q11.23 — Incorrect. This is Williams syndrome.
- C. 15q11-q13 paternal loss — Incorrect. This is associated with Prader-Willi syndrome.
- D. 22q11.2 deletion — Correct. This is the classic chromosome abnormality.
- E. 5p — Incorrect. This causes cri-du-chat syndrome.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- DiGeorge/22q11.2 deletion: cardiac anomalies, abnormal facies, thymic hypoplasia, cleft palate, hypocalcemia.
- T-cell immunodeficiency may occur due to thymic hypoplasia/aplasia.
- Confirm with appropriate genetic testing.

questions.stem: In the classic CATCH-22 mnemonic for DiGeorge syndrome, which feature corresponds to “T”?
questions.correctAnswerText: Thymic hypoplasia or aplasia
questions.initialExplanation: CATCH-22 summarizes cardiac defects, abnormal facies, thymic hypoplasia, cleft palate, and hypocalcemia associated with 22q11.2 deletion.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Tracheal atresia — Incorrect. This is not the mnemonic feature.
- B. Thrombocytopenia — Incorrect. This is not the “T” in CATCH-22.
- C. Thymic hypoplasia/aplasia — Correct. This can cause T-cell immunodeficiency.
- D. Tall stature — Incorrect. This is not a defining feature.
- E. Thyrotoxicosis — Incorrect. This is not the mnemonic feature.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- C: cardiac defects.
- A: abnormal facies.
- T: thymic hypoplasia.
- C: cleft palate.
- H: hypocalcemia due to parathyroid hypoplasia.
- “22” refers to chromosome 22q11.2 deletion.

questions.stem: A child with suspected DiGeorge syndrome has recurrent infections and seizures. Which combination of investigations is particularly relevant?

options.label: D
options.text: Calcium, parathyroid hormone, immune/T-cell assessment, echocardiography, and genetic testing

questions.correctAnswerText: Calcium, parathyroid hormone, immune/T-cell assessment, echocardiography, and genetic testing
questions.initialExplanation: DiGeorge syndrome may involve hypocalcemia, T-cell immunodeficiency, and congenital heart disease; genetic testing confirms the deletion.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Trisomy 21 testing — Incorrect. DiGeorge syndrome is associated with 22q11.2 deletion.

- B. Cystic fibrosis tests — Incorrect. These assess a different disease.
- C. Ferritin only — Incorrect. This does not assess the major DiGeorge manifestations.
- D. Multisystem assessment — Correct. It evaluates the principal associated complications.
- E. Renal tests — Incorrect. They do not evaluate the main suspected syndrome.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Check calcium and PTH in suspected hypocalcemia.
- Assess T-cell number/function and infection history.
- Evaluate congenital heart disease and confirm the genetic diagnosis.

## Dysmorphology and Pedigree

questions.stem: What does dysmorphology refer to?

options.label: C
options.text: The measurement of blood pressure in infants

options.label: E
options.text: The study and assessment of abnormal physical form and congenital anomalies

questions.correctAnswerText: The study and assessment of abnormal physical form and congenital anomalies
questions.initialExplanation: Dysmorphology evaluates unusual physical features and congenital anomalies that may arise during embryonic development.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Muscle power — Incorrect. This is part of neurological examination.
- B. Bacterial morphology — Incorrect. This is microbiology.
- C. Blood pressure — Incorrect. This is a vital sign.
- D. Anemia — Incorrect. This is a hematological condition.

- E. Abnormal form — Correct. This is the definition.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Dysmorphic features may be isolated or part of a syndrome.
- Assess the whole child and look for a pattern of anomalies.
- A careful family history and pedigree may support diagnosis.

questions.stem: A congenital structural defect caused by an intrinsic abnormal developmental process in an organ or tissue is termed:
questions.correctAnswerText: Malformation
questions.initialExplanation: A malformation is a primary structural defect arising during development of the tissue or organ itself.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Deformation — Incorrect. This results from abnormal mechanical forces acting on a normally formed structure.
- B. Malformation — Correct. Examples include cleft lip/palate and many congenital heart defects.
- C. Sequence — Incorrect. This is a cascade of secondary anomalies following one primary defect.
- D. Association — Incorrect. This is a non-random pattern of anomalies without one established unifying cause.

- E. Disruption — Incorrect. This is destruction of a previously normal structure, e.g. amniotic band disruption.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Malformation = intrinsic developmental error.
- Deformation = mechanical distortion.
