- Disruption = breakdown/destruction of a previously normal structure.

questions.stem: Severe oligohydramnios causes persistent joint contractures and pulmonary hypoplasia by restricting fetal movement and space. This is best classified as:
questions.correctAnswerText: Deformation
questions.initialExplanation: Deformation results from abnormal mechanical forces affecting a structure that was initially developing normally.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Imprinting defect — Incorrect. This alters parent-of-origin gene expression.

- B. Aneuploidy — Incorrect. This is an abnormal chromosome number.
- C. Disruption — Incorrect. This is destruction of previously normal tissue, such as by an amniotic band.
- D. Malformation — Incorrect. This is an intrinsic primary developmental defect.
- E. Deformation — Correct. Oligohydramnios can mechanically restrict fetal movement and distort developing structures.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Deformation often results from mechanical forces.
- Oligohydramnios can cause positional deformities and pulmonary hypoplasia.
- The underlying tissue may have developed normally before the external force.

questions.stem: An amniotic band encircles a fetal digit and causes constriction and distal amputation. This is an example of:
questions.correctAnswerText: Disruption
questions.initialExplanation: Disruption is the destruction of a previously normally developing structure by an external process.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Malformation — Incorrect. This arises from an intrinsic developmental error.
- B. Polyploidy — Incorrect. This is an extra whole chromosome set.

- C. Disruption — Correct. Amniotic bands can constrict and damage a previously formed part.
- D. Deformation — Incorrect. This is distortion by mechanical forces without destructive interruption.
- E. Sequence — Incorrect. This is a cascade of defects caused by one primary anomaly.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Disruption = destruction of previously normal tissue.
- Amniotic band sequence can cause constriction rings and amputations.
- Infection can also disrupt previously normal fetal tissues.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes a sequence from a syndrome?

options.label: A
options.text: A syndrome contains one minor anomaly

options.label: B
options.text: A sequence is typically a chromosome number abnormality; a syndrome is typically multifactorial

options.label: C
options.text: Both terms mean exactly the same thing

options.label: D
options.text: A sequence is a cascade of secondary anomalies from one primary defect; a syndrome is a consistent pattern of anomalies due to a known underlying cause

options.label: E
options.text: A sequence is caused by parental consanguinity

questions.correctAnswerText: A sequence is a cascade of secondary anomalies from one primary defect; a syndrome is a consistent pattern of anomalies due to a known underlying cause
questions.initialExplanation: A sequence describes a chain of consequences from one initiating anomaly, whereas a syndrome describes a recognizable pattern of multiple anomalies with a common cause.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. One minor anomaly — Incorrect. A syndrome generally describes a pattern of multiple features.
- B. Chromosome-only — Incorrect. Neither term is restricted to chromosomal abnormalities.
- C. Same meaning — Incorrect. They describe different concepts.
- D. Correct distinction — Correct. This is the key dysmorphology distinction.
- E. Consanguinity only — Incorrect. A sequence is not defined by consanguinity.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Sequence: one primary defect causes secondary effects (e.g. Pierre Robin sequence).
- Syndrome: consistent pattern from a common cause (e.g. Down syndrome).
- Association: non-random group of anomalies without a fully established single cause.

questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes a major congenital anomaly from a minor anomaly?

options.label: A
options.text: A major anomaly is typically visible on the skin

options.label: B
options.text: Minor anomalies not usually occur in genetic syndromes

options.label: C
options.text: Major anomalies are typically inherited as autosomal dominant traits

options.label: D
options.text: A minor anomaly typically indicates a severe chromosomal disorder

options.label: E
options.text: A major anomaly has significant medical, functional, or surgical consequences; a minor anomaly usually has limited medical effect

questions.correctAnswerText: A major anomaly has significant medical, functional, or surgical consequences; a minor anomaly usually has limited medical effect
questions.initialExplanation: Major anomalies generally require medical or surgical intervention, while minor anomalies are unusual physical findings with limited functional impact but may contribute to a dysmorphic pattern.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Skin only — Incorrect. Major anomalies can involve any organ system.
- B. Never in syndromes — Incorrect. Minor anomalies may cluster and help identify a syndrome.
- C. Always AD — Incorrect. Major anomalies can arise from chromosomal, single-gene, multifactorial, environmental, or unknown causes.

- D. Always severe — Incorrect. A minor anomaly alone does not prove a severe genetic disorder.
- E. Functional significance — Correct. This is the practical distinction used.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Count and characterize congenital anomalies.
- Multiple minor anomalies may prompt evaluation for an underlying syndrome.
- A major anomaly warrants appropriate clinical assessment regardless of genetic suspicion.

questions.stem: A newborn has features suggestive of Down syndrome. Which karyotype represents the common free-trisomy form?
questions.initialExplanation: Free trisomy 21 is represented by 47 chromosomes with an additional chromosome 21.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct: 47,XX,+21 represents a female with trisomy 21.
- B. Incorrect: A 5p deletion is associated with Cri-du-chat syndrome.

- C. Incorrect: 45,X is Turner syndrome.
- D. Incorrect: 46,XX is a normal female karyotype.

questions.highYieldPoints:
- Down syndrome is most commonly due to trisomy 21.
- Translocation and mosaic forms have different recurrence-counselling implications.

questions.stem: A boy has obesity, hyperphagia, hypogonadism and developmental difficulties. Testing identifies loss of expression of paternally derived genes on chromosome 15. Which syndrome is most likely?
questions.correctAnswerText: Prader–Willi syndrome
questions.initialExplanation: Prader–Willi syndrome is associated with loss of paternal gene expression in the relevant chromosome 15 region.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct: Prader–Willi syndrome is associated with loss of paternal expression and features including hyperphagia and obesity.
- B. Incorrect: Turner syndrome results from complete/partial absence of one X chromosome.

- C. Incorrect: Williams syndrome is associated with a 7q11.23 microdeletion.
- D. Incorrect: Fragile X is associated with FMR1 expansion.
- E. Incorrect: Angelman syndrome is associated with loss of maternal UBE3A expression in the relevant region.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Prader–Willi: paternal 15q11–q13 expression loss; hyperphagia and obesity.
- Angelman: maternal expression loss; severe developmental and speech impairment, ataxia and seizures.

questions.stem: A boy has intellectual disability, a long face, large ears and post-pubertal macro-orchidism. Which genetic mechanism is most likely?

options.label: D
options.text: CGG repeat expansion in FMR1 with abnormal methylation

questions.correctAnswerText: CGG repeat expansion in FMR1 with abnormal methylation
questions.initialExplanation: Fragile X syndrome is caused by CGG repeat expansion in FMR1, usually leading to gene silencing through methylation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect: 45,X causes Turner syndrome.

- B. Incorrect: Paternal 15q loss causes Prader–Willi syndrome.
- C. Incorrect: 7q11.23 microdeletion causes Williams syndrome.
- D. Correct: FMR1 CGG expansion is the defining molecular mechanism of Fragile X.
- E. Incorrect: Trisomy 21 causes Down syndrome.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Fragile X is an X-linked trinucleotide repeat disorder.
- The phenotype often includes characteristic facial features and macro-orchidism.

questions.stem: A woman with a mitochondrial DNA disorder asks about transmission to her children. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Mitochondrial DNA is transmitted through the maternal line

options.label: B
options.text: Affected fathers transmit mitochondrial DNA to most sons

options.label: D
options.text: Mitochondrial DNA is inherited from both parents equally

questions.correctAnswerText: Mitochondrial DNA is transmitted through the maternal line
questions.initialExplanation: Mitochondrial DNA is maternally inherited because the ovum provides the cytoplasmic material to the embryo.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct: Mitochondrial DNA is transmitted through the mother.
- B. Incorrect: Paternal mitochondrial inheritance is not the usual pattern described.
- C. Incorrect: This is not autosomal dominant nuclear inheritance.
- D. Incorrect: Mitochondrial inheritance is not biparental in the standard pattern.

- E. Incorrect: Both sons and daughters can inherit mitochondrial DNA variants from an affected mother.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Mitochondrial inheritance is maternal.
- All children of an affected mother may be at risk, with variable heteroplasmy and expression.
